brief.situation: 10:10 in the emergency department. You are the nurse in a monitored room. Mr. Okafor, 74, came in by ambulance after nearly fainting at the grocery store. He is pale and says he feels 'washed out'.
handover: Triage: ESI 2. Heart rate 40, blood pressure 102/58, SpO2 96% on room air, alert.

The department's symptomatic bradycardia standing order: monitor, IV access, a 12-lead ECG, transcutaneous pacing pads applied, the ordered atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, and the physician called to the bedside for any sign of instability.
His home medication list includes metoprolol, due at 10:00. The emergency physician is in the next room and comes when called.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and treat as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: The block worsens without treatment. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

Atropine gives little: a block below the AV node does not respond, so instability still comes. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

The authored point of instability: hypotension and confusion. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

The authored point of an asystolic pause. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.
The physician called to the bedside within 5 minutes of the first sign of instability (department practice).
Atropine within 5 minutes of reaching the room (department practice).
A focused assessment or question: about 1 min.
About 10 minutes for the physician to start transcutaneous pacing and call cardiology for a transvenous wire; a floor bed about 10 minutes.

An AV nodal blocking drug given into a complete heart block: a long pause within about 2 minutes. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

why.question: Mr. Okafor's pressure is falling and he is confused. What is happening, and what do you do?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: Complete heart block with a slow wide escape; hypotension and altered mental status make it unstable; atropine often fails below the AV node.
parts.modelAnswer: Complete heart block with a wide escape at the low thirties. He is now hypotensive and confused, so this is unstable bradycardia, and atropine hasn't helped.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Physician to the bedside now for transcutaneous pacing (pads already on); hold every AV nodal blocker; hand off the metoprolol history.
parts.modelAnswer: Get the physician now for transcutaneous pacing on the pads, hold the metoprolol and anything else that slows the node, and tell them about the extra dose yesterday.

expertPath.text: Pacing pads on; atropine as ordered.
Physician to the bedside for transcutaneous pacing; metoprolol held; hand off.

unsafe.headline: A beta-blocker into heart block
unsafe.body: A scheduled home dose is not automatic. A slow, symptomatic rhythm means every AV nodal blocker is held and the prescriber asked.

worsened.headline: Asystolic pause
worsened.body: Symptomatic bradycardia that atropine doesn't fix needs pacing. Instability (hypotension, confusion, shock, chest pain, heart failure) is the trigger to call.

wrongRoute.headline: Moved without pacing
wrongRoute.body: An unstable complete heart block does not go to a floor bed to wait for the morning.

target.headline: Paced in time
target.body: Pads on early, atropine as ordered, the ECG read, and instability called at once. That is the expert path.

recovered.headline: Paced, with delays
recovered.body: Check how soon the atropine went in and how long the hypotension and confusion lasted before the call.

time_up.headline: Still bradycardic
time_up.body: Unstable bradycardia needs pacing within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: A heart rate of 40 with near-fainting is symptomatic bradycardia: pads on, the ordered atropine, and a 12-lead ECG, which shows complete heart block with a wide escape. Atropine often does little below the AV node. When the pressure falls and he becomes confused, that is instability: the physician comes now for transcutaneous pacing. His metoprolol is held, and the extra dose yesterday goes in the hand-off.

paceQ.ask: While the team takes over: atropine hasn't helped an unstable patient. What comes next?

choices.label: Transcutaneous pacing (or a dopamine or epinephrine infusion)
Wait and repeat the ECG in an hour
A beta-blocker to steady the rhythm

paceQ.explain: Transcutaneous pacing is the key escalation for persistent symptomatic bradycardia after atropine, with dopamine or epinephrine infusions as the alternative.

unstQ.ask: While you assess: which finding makes a bradycardia unstable?
unstQ.explain: Unstable bradycardia is defined by hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure, not by the rate alone.
